Note:

1. The substrate of Indirect Immunofluorescence is Human Epithelial Cell line HEp-20-10 and Primate (Monkey) Liver Cell Line.

2. Class of Antibody: IgG class of Gamma Globulins directed against nuclear and cellular components.

3. Primary dilution of the performed test: 1 in 100.

Comment:

1. Indirect Immunofluorescence (IFA) test is a gold standard screening test for Anti-nuclear Antibodies. It is a sensitive test for the detection of serum antibodies that react specifically with various cellular proteins and nucleic acids.

2. A negative ANA test virtually rules out a diagnosis of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus but a positive test may be indicative of a number of autoimmune

connective tissue diseases such as Scleroderma (Systemic Sclerosis), Discoid Lupus Erythematosus, Drug-Induced Lupus, Mixed Connective tissue

Disease, Rheumatoid Arthritis, Sjogren's syndrome, CREST Syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, Oesophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly,

Telangiectasia), Polymyositis and Dermatomyositis.

3. When correlated with the Clinical history, physical examination and other laboratory findings, it identifies almost all patients with SLE.

4. Population studies show positive ANA in approximately 1 to 5 % of healthy subjects. Up to 40 % of elderly subjects with the chronic nonrheumatological illness have ANA positivity usually at low titre.

5. False-positive results for ANA can be seen in patients taking certain medications like Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Procainamide, Phenytoin, Penicillin etc.

Pathological conditions like Neoplasm, Chronic Liver Disease, Viral illness and Chronic Infection, may result in low titre of ANA.

6. Patients with SLE receiving steroids may have negative test results. If results are negative and clinical features are suspected, recommendation is to repeat the ANA IFA test after 2-3 months.

7. ANA testing is not used to track or monitor the clinical course of SLE, thus serial ANA tests for diagnosed patients are not commonly ordered.

8. There is no absolute cut off at which an ANA is clinically significant, however the higher the ANA titre the more likely it is to be associated with Systemic

Rheumatic disease. In general ANA positivity of greater than or equal to 1:160 titre is of clinical significance in the diagnosis of Collagen Vascular Disorders.

9. The positivity seen on fluorescence indicates:

1+ = Minimum Immunofluorescence of no significance.

2+ = Mildly positive, clinically insignificant.

3+ = Significant positive, needs clinical correlation.

4+ = Strong positive, highly suggestive of collagen vascular disease.

10. In the case of a positive screening result, confirmation is recommended by using a Mono-specific ELISA or Immunoblot profile or Panel to detect specific antibodies present in the sample.

Interpretation Guidelines (Sample screening Dilution - 1:100):

Negative : No Immunofluorescence

+ : Weak Positive (1:100)

++ : Moderate Positive (1:320)

+++ : Strong Positive (1:1000)

++++ : Very strong Positive (1:3200)

 

Test Description:

Antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) are unusual antibodies, detectable in the blood, that have the capability of binding to certain

structures within the nucleus of the cells. ANAs indicate the possible presence of autoimmunity & provide, therefore, an indication of autoimmune illness. Fluorescence tech. are frequently used to actually detect the antibodies in the cells, thus ANA testing is sometimes referred to as fluorescent antinuclear antibody test (FANA). The ANA test is a sensitive screening test used to detect autoimmune diseases.

 

Technique:

 

Indirect Immunofluorescence

 

The BIOCHIP Slide is a combination of Hep-20-10 cells and primate liver and has the following advantages.

 

•   It is a global standard tech. with a natural antigen spectrum capable of detecting more than 30 diagnostically relevant auto

    antibodies.

•   Hep 20-10 cell lines contain 40% mitotic cells, facilitating easier identification of rare patterns.

•   If the test is negative, detectable level of auto antibodies is ruled out. In case of a positive result, autoantibodies against any

    one or in some cases simultaneously against more than one antigens may be present and further monospecific tests or

    panel of profiles can be used to determine the specific autoantibodies present.

•  NOTE- All weak positive (+) results may be repeated after 6 - 8 weeks.

 

Associated Tests: Monospecific ELISA to define single antigens, ANA Immunoblot assay.

 

Abbreviations: SLE: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, SCL: Scleroderma, MCTD: Mixed Connective Tissue Disease; CFS: Chronic

Fatigue Syndrome; AIH: Autoimmune Hepatitis, PBC: Primary Bilary Cirrhosis, PM:Polymyositis, DM:Dermatomyositis, SS: Systemic sclerosis, RA:Rheumatoid Arthritis

Immuno fluorescence Analysis

 

Antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) are unusual antibodies, detectable in the blood, that have the capacity of binding to certain structures within the nucleus of the cells. ANAs indicate the possible presence of autoimmunity and provide an indication for doctors to consider the possibility of autoimmune illness. ANAs can be found in approximately 5% of the normal population, usually in low titers (low levels). These persons usually have no disease. Titers of lower than 1:80 are likely to be insignificant. (ANA titers of less than or equal to 1:40 are considered negative). Even higher titers are often insignificant in patients over 60 years of age. Some older adults (5% to 40%) may have mildly elevated levels. Older women appear to have higher ANA titers than older men. ANAs are found in patients with a number of different autoimmune diseases, such as: systematic lupus erythematosus, Sjogren’s syndrome-Rheumatoid arthritis, Polymyositis, Scleroderma, Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, Juvenile Diabetes mellitus, Addison disease, Pernicious anemia and Glomerulonephritis. ANAs can also be produced in patients with infections (virus or bacteria), Lung diseases (primary pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension), Gastrointestinal diseases (ulcerative colitis, Crohn’s disease, primary billary cirrhiosis , alcoholic liver disease), Blood disorders (idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, hemolytic anemia), Cancers (melanoma, breast, lung, kidney, ovarian and others), Skin diseases (psoriasis, pemphigus), etc. Many medications can sometimes stimulate the production of ANAs, these are referred to as drug-induced ANAs. These medications include certain anticonvulsants (ex.Dilantin) : certain antibiotics (ex. Isoniazid, penicillin, and Tetracycline), birth control pills, lithium, and some diuretics, such as chlorthalidone (Hygroton) and certain heart or blood pressure medications, such as acebutolol (Sectral), captropril (Capoten), atenolol (Tenormin),metoprolol (Lopressor), lovastatine (Mevacor),and quinidine.

The result of an antinuclear antibody (ANA) test is used along with a thorough medical history, physical examination or other tests to diagnose autoimmune diseases. Autoimmune diseases cannot be diagnosed by the  results of the ANA test alone.

ANAs present different patterns depending on the staining of the cell nucleus in the laboratory : homogeneous or diffuse: speckled: nucleolar: and peripheral or rim. While these patterns are not specific for any one illness, certain illnesses can more frequently be associated with one pattern or another. The patterns then can sometimes give the doctor further clues as to types of illnesses to look for in evaluating a patient. For example, the nucleolar pattern is more commonly seen in the disease scleroderma. All inconclusive patterns of IFA positives not correlating with the clinical suspicion need to confirm by testing for antibodies to Extractable Nuclear Antigens (ENAs). One can either test for these by ANA panel (9 antigens) by immunoblot or test for individual antibodies by SMC enabled ELISAs.
